extraction.name: MMMU
extraction.description: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI. MMMU includes 11.5K carefully selected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines, 30 subjects, 183 subfields, and 30 heterogeneous image types to evaluate multimodal models on college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.citeAs: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was curated in three stages. First, the authors went through common university majors to decide which subjects to include, selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on whether visual inputs are commonly adopted and ruling out subjects like law and linguistics. Second, they recruited over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources and to create new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoid sources prohibiting copy and redistribution, and select questions without immediately available answers to reduce data contamination concerns. This resulted in a diverse collection of 13K questions from various sources. The final benchmark contains 11.5K questions after quality control.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Others
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions were sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, lecture materials, free online resources, and other study materials. The paper also states that annotators collected multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data quality control involved lexical overlap and source URL similarity to identify potential duplicate problems, followed by author review to eliminate duplications. Problems were then distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format. In the final stage, authors categorized problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems classified as very easy and not aligning with the design criteria were excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All questions were required to contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, and be answerable with one of the given options or a short answer. Annotators clearly categorized each question as multiple-choice or open-ended and annotated fields including question text, answer options, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation if available. The structured JSON format included fields for number, question type, question text, answer options, correct answer, question difficulty, and explanation. Images were inserted as file paths in the question, options, or explanations. A secondary review team rigorously vetted annotations, and regular audits of random samples were conducted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors served as annotators to collect multimodal questions. They collected questions from textbooks and online resources and created new questions based on their expertise where necessary. The annotation protocol required accurate and consistent annotations with academic rigor. Questions had to contain one or more images, be in English, be college-level, and be unambiguous. Annotators labeled question type, question text, answer options for multiple-choice questions, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation if available. Ambiguities were flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings to establish a standardized approach.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: a user-friendly web interface for data annotation and verification
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A secondary review team rigorously vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence, and regular audits of random samples were conducted to ensure sustained quality and consistency. Ambiguous or unclear instances were flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings. The authors also analyzed 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V error instances using expert annotators who identified root causes of mispredictions based on their knowledge and golden explanations if available. The paper reports 2% annotation error among these analyzed model errors.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors and various disciplines and subjects. The paper also states the questions were manually collected by a team of 50 college students from various disciplines and subjects.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The appendix includes a version change log. Changes to V2 (Dec.18) from V1 (Nov.27), changes to V3 (Dec.21) from V2 (Dec.18), and changes to V4 (June.13) from V3 (Dec.21) are documented. Xiang Yue took the lead in the dataset release.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The annotation protocol states that annotators should avoid collecting questions that contain any private information. The dataset includes subject matter involving age and gender in some questions and includes medical and health-related images and content.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that monitoring progress toward Expert AGI is of both intellectual and societal importance because Expert AGI could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The authors believe MMMU will be instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitoring progress towards Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The paper also notes that GPT-4V often exhibits a bias towards text, prioritizing textual information over visual inputs.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper cautions that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and the 90th percentile of skilled adults, nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. It also states that the manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. The few-shot analysis suggests existing open-source models' few-shot learning ability is very weak and that the data samples might be too hard for these models to understand the underlying patterns or context.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The benchmark is designed to evaluate multimodal models on college-level multi-discipline multimodal understanding and reasoning, measuring perception, knowledge, and reasoning. It is divided into a few-shot development set, a validation set useful for hyperparameter selection, and a test set. The authors evaluate models in zero-shot settings and also report few-shot results for selected models in the appendix.
